card.hook: Here's a fun one: the whole Chicago skyline gets squished into a giant shiny bean, and you get to stand right next to it. Expect company, so bring a little patience.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Cloud Gate (the Bean), at its north or south end, and frame the curved mirror surface with the skyline and sky reflected in it. For a wider view of the park, walk to the ledge on the west side overlooking the skating rink.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the Bean and its reflection. From the west-side ledge, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit in the rink, the sculpture and the skyline, then try zoom 2x or more for a tighter crop of the reflected buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the reflection, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late evening is best if you want fewer people in your shot. One guide says late afternoon light is best, so try more than one visit if you can.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the west side of Cloud Gate looking toward Michigan Avenue, so the Bean is behind you and the high-rises squeeze into the frame too. Use the front camera, or try the outer corner where the steel meets the plaza for a shot with buildings behind and usually fewer people.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps out in front of the Bean and shoot from a long angle, while you stand central with the whole sculpture behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Admission is free and the park is a public space, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any work or closures around the Bean and its plaza.
card.challenge: Take a few frames and find the one where you can spot yourself, tiny and wobbly, in the Bean's curve.
card.good_to_know: Millennium Park opened in July 2004 and covers about 24.5 acres in the north-west corner of Grant Park. It sits on top of parking garages and rail lines, so it's described as the world's largest rooftop garden. It was Chicago's top tourist destination in 2017.

selfie_research.notes: I treated the Bean (Cloud Gate, in Grainger/AT&T Plaza) as the landmark, since it is the main photo draw in Millennium Park. card.hook: Stand at the bottom of Willis Tower, tip your head back, and watch the dark lines race up and out of sight. Locals still call it the Sears Tower, and from down here it feels like it's earned any name it likes.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits right on Willis Tower's footprint, so you'll be looking almost straight up at the building. For the whole tower, walk back to the far side of the surrounding streets (Franklin Street, Jackson Boulevard, Wacker Drive or Adams Street) and shoot from there.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x at the base to fit in the full height, then 1x from across the street. If your phone has 2x or 5x, save it for the stepped top section.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tilt up slowly and keep a little sky above the top.
card.best_time: Clear daytime gives you crisp lines and bright sky. Early morning or late afternoon can add some warmth to the glass, and after dusk you can use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post.
card.selfie_here: The Ledge on the Skydeck (103rd floor) is the top photo spot in the tower, those glass boxes sticking out from the building. Use the front camera and remember that here the tower is what you're standing on, not what's behind you. For a classic one outside, try the front camera at 0.5x with the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the northeast corner of N Franklin St and W Wacker Drive facing south toward the tower, and ask your passer-by to stand on the sidewalk between you and the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: The streets around the tower are public, but the Skydeck and the building's interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go. The Ledge needs a paid ticket and there may be long lines.
card.challenge: Find a street lamp or a passer-by to put in the foreground, then see if you can make the tower look even bigger next to them.
card.good_to_know: Willis Tower is 110 storeys and 1,451 feet (442.3 m) tall. It opened in 1973 as the world's tallest building and kept the title for nearly 25 years. It's still the tallest building in Chicago, and its Skydeck draws more than 1.7 million visitors a year.

card.hook: You walk up to the biggest mirror in Chicago and suddenly you're in the shot, tiny, grinning, and bent like a funhouse version of yourself. That's The Bean, and it's the whole point.
card.stand_here: Head for the west side of the Bean, on Grainger Plaza (formerly AT&T Plaza), and face the steel. From there the Loop skyline sits right in the curve of the sculpture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the skyline reflection. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you're close to the steel or under the arch, and try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out one building or a patch of reflected sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the reflected skyline, then slide it a little darker so the bright steel and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds build. You'll get cleaner reflections and fewer people walking through your frame. Midday sun can cause glare on the steel, and it gets busy from late morning.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the west side of the Bean, facing Michigan Avenue, so the reflection picks up nearby towers like the Aon Center and the Chicago Cultural Center behind you. Use the front camera, hold it low and close to your body, and let the steel do the rest. For a wilder one, walk under the arch to the middle of the underside and shoot upward, where you and the crowd bend into kaleidoscope shapes.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stay back across the plaza while you stand close to the front of the Bean, and have them shoot wide so the whole sculpture and the skyline fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: If lightning is in the area, security may close that part of the park and push visitors back about 50 feet. Work around the plaza can affect access, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Find your own reflection, then take a photo where you can spot yourself, the skyline and a cloud all in one swirl.
card.good_to_know: The Bean's real name is Cloud Gate, and it's by Anish Kapoor. It was built between 2004 and 2006 and dedicated on 15 May 2006. It's made of 168 steel plates joined so smoothly you can't see a seam, and its shape was inspired by liquid mercury. It measures about 10 by 20 by 13 m.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the west side of the Bean, on Grainger Plaza (formerly AT&T Plaza), and face the steel. From there the Loop skyline sits right in the curve of the sculpture.

selfie_spots.detail: Walk under the arch to the middle of the curved underside, where the surface is most concave, and shoot upward.
selfie_spots.why: The curved underside bends reflections of you and the people around you into kaleidoscopic shapes, and fewer visitors bother to walk under it.

card.hook: Most people hit the middle of Navy Pier, get swallowed by nine million of their closest friends, and call it a day. Keep walking to the far end and you get open water on several sides and a lot more elbow room.
card.stand_here: Walk about 400 m further east from the pier entrance to the tip of Navy Pier, out over the lake. Turn around and face back toward the land, so the pier's buildings and the city skyline sit behind the railings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the water, the pier and the skyline into one big shot. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the skyline in closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, tap the skyline, and slide it darker if the sky looks too bright.
card.best_time: Sunset is the popular pick. If you want fewer people around you, go early in the morning. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep things steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand on either the north or south side of Pier Park with the Centennial Wheel and carousel behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold the phone a little high. For a quick one at the entrance, stand in front of the stone wall with the "Navy Pier" lettering, right beside the Chicago Children's Museum.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn by the fountain in Polk Bros Park, just outside the Chicago Children's Museum, and shoot back toward the pier while you stand with the pier behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones aren't allowed on the pier property, and rides and events may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go. One old forum post says a few quick photos are fine but lingering in one spot isn't. That's just one person's account, so double-check.
card.challenge: Use the railing as a guide line, keep the horizon dead level, and get the whole length of the pier in one frame. Bonus points if you look like you meant to do it.
card.good_to_know: Navy Pier is 3,300 feet (1,010 m) long and covers over 50 acres of shops, restaurants, theatres, gardens and parks. It opened on 15 July 1916 as Municipal Pier and was renamed in 1927 to honour naval veterans of the First World War. The Centennial Wheel opened in May 2016 and stands 196 feet tall.

card.hook: This museum has the best front lawn in Chicago, and it knows it. A long white marble facade, trees and water on one side, and the skyline behind: you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand in Museum Campus, on the lawns and reflection-pool area in front of the Field Museum. The museum is to the north-west, about 4 minutes on foot, so face it and step back until the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full front with some lawn or water in front. Try 0.5x if you're close or want more of the reflection pool, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the columns and carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, when the light from the west falls on the building. The grounds can be busy, so take a few shots and wait for a gap in the crowd, or step a bit further back where fewer people walk through.
card.selfie_here: Climb the front steps of the Field Museum, turn your back to the entrance and use the front camera so the building and columns frame you. If your phone has 0.5x on the front camera, use it to fit more of the facade in. For another backdrop, try the paved paths of the Museum Campus Prairie directly behind the museum, where the facade is visible on one side.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the museum in the distance, try the lower-level lakeside promenade near Soldier Field, where the museum sits at a lower elevation, and ask a passer-by to take your photo there.
card.rules_and_safety: The lawns and grounds are fine to photograph from outside, but the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go. One travel blog says selfie sticks are sometimes allowed inside if you don't block views or other guests, but that isn't an official rule, so check at the entrance.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the columns are dead straight, then one where a tree or the reflection pool frames the whole building. Which do you like more?
card.good_to_know: The museum began with the artefacts shown at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. It's named after its first major benefactor, department-store owner Marshall Field. It moved here in 1921 from its first home in Jackson Park.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Museum Campus, on the lawns and reflection-pool area in front of the Field Museum. The museum is to the north-west, about 4 minutes on foot, so face it and step back until the whole building fits.

card.hook: Two bronze lions have been guarding this front door for ages, and sometimes they turn up dressed for a holiday or a big game. Either way, they're the easiest foreground you'll find in Chicago.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk at the corner of South Michigan Avenue and East Adams Street, across Michigan Avenue from the main entrance, and face east. The museum itself is about 1 minute on foot from there, to the east. Step back toward the kerb so the lions, the steps and the entrance all fit with the city around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the facade, the grand staircase and both lions in one shot. If the pavement is crowded, 1x gives a more natural view. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the lions and the main doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the lions low in the frame with the staircase behind them, and line up the building's vertical edges with the grid so it stands straight.
card.best_time: The light on the facade changes through the day, so take a look at how it falls when you arrive. This corner is busy, so wait a moment for a gap in the people on the steps, and take a few frames because folks keep walking through.
card.selfie_here: Go up to the top landing of the front steps and stand beside one of the two bronze lions, with the museum entrance behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front, and hold your arm out so the doorway fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Michigan Avenue sidewalk at East Adams Street facing the lions, while you pose by a lion so they can fit you, the lions and the staircase rising above.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are banned in the museum, its gardens and the public spaces around it, including the lion steps and South Garden, so use your arm. The lions were once taken away for conservation work, so check they're on their plinths before you go.
card.challenge: Get a photo where the lion looks like it's guarding you, with the whole staircase behind it and nobody walking through the shot.
card.good_to_know: The Art Institute of Chicago was founded in 1879 and is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States. The main building was put up for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and Renzo Piano's Modern Wing, opened in 2009, made the museum much bigger. Inside you'll find Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte and Hopper's Nighthawks.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: the best pictures of Shedd Aquarium are the ones you take before you go in. Outside, you get columns, a dome and the whole Chicago lakefront. Inside, you get dim rooms and a lot of blurry fish.
card.stand_here: Stand in Northerly Island Park, at the point beside the Adler Planetarium, and face north-west across the water. The skyline fills the view, with the lakefront in front, and the aquarium is just along the shore in that same direction.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the skyline and lakefront. Try 0.5x for more water and sky, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the distant towers closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the skyline, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out, and turn on gridlines so the horizon sits on the lower line.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water. Quieter times of day also make it easier to find a clear spot on the steps.
card.selfie_here: Head to the north steps of Shedd Aquarium, outside at the entrance. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone offers it), with the columns on one side and the lake on the other, so the columned front is behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stay on the Museum Campus lawn between Shedd and the Field Museum at a mid-distance, while you stand on the lawn with both buildings in view and the lakefront behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the aquarium, and selfie sticks are restricted in many galleries. Rules can change, so check the current visitor rules before you go in.
card.challenge: Find the tiny dolphins, waves and shells carved into the stonework, then get one in the frame with you.
card.good_to_know: Shedd Aquarium opened on 30 May 1930 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1987. The central block is octagonal, with Doric columns across the front, a formal staircase and a dome on top. It sits on the Museum Campus beside the Field Museum and the Adler Planetarium.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Northerly Island Park, at the point beside the Adler Planetarium, and face north-west across the water. The skyline fills the view, with the lakefront in front, and the aquarium is just along the shore in that same direction.

card.hook: Most city photos fight the crowds. The Chicago Riverwalk hands you a wide strip of water to shoot across, so you get a clean view of the Wrigley Building's terracotta front with the skyline piled up behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the river-side walkway opposite DuSable Bridge, on the side away from the Wrigley Building. The Riverwalk itself lies to the north-west of this point. Face across the river to the Wrigley Building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the Wrigley Building and the skyline across the water. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the terracotta details and upper floors. Use 0.5x at Wells Street Bridge or the memorial plaza, when you want lots in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the Wrigley Building on one third of the frame, then tap it and slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Blue hour, the 20-30 minutes after sunset, is recommended for glowing light and reflections near DuSable Bridge. Early morning is calmer, with lighter traffic on the bridges, according to one photographer.
card.selfie_here: Try the wide, cascading River Theater steps near Clark Street. They lead right down to the water, so the Riverwalk and river sit behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and check the map for the exact spot. Another option is the walkway that juts out across from River Roast, which gives an open view of the river and city behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Riverwalk while you stand on Wells Street Bridge (299 North Wells St), then check the framing on the spot to make sure you're the star.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal handheld photography needs no permit in Chicago's parks during park hours. Parts of the Riverwalk may close at times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a tour boat to slide across the water in front of the Wrigley Building, then snap it so the boat and the terracotta both make the shot.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 2001 as part of the Wacker Drive rebuild, when the road was moved to make room for the walk. The Vietnam Veterans Memorial Plaza was built in 2005, with terraces, a waterfall and a pool. The newer sections from State Street to Lake Street opened in 2015 and 2016.

card.hook: The John Hancock Center is 100 storeys of dark, no-nonsense tower, and it looks smaller on your phone screen than it does in real life. Plan on a few tries.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, right at the tower at 875 North Michigan Avenue on the Magnificent Mile. Face the building and point your phone up. For more of the tower in the frame, walk back along the pavement until it fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in as much tower as you can, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for picking out details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean, and tap the building then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't go white.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is best, when the light is softer and the sky is easier to handle. After dusk, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the alley just east of the tower, use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt up so the tower rises behind your shoulder between the buildings. If you're over in Lincoln Park, the wooden pavilion by the Zoo's South Pond frames the skyline with the Hancock behind you, though that's a separate spot from the tower.
card.ask_someone: Take the stairs down from Michigan Avenue to river level near the Michigan Avenue Bridge, stand there yourself, and ask a passer-by to shoot you with the tower rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the tower from the pavement, but the observation deck is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone steady against passers-by on the busy pavement.
card.challenge: Take one shot where both edges of the tower sit perfectly on the gridlines, with a passer-by at the bottom for scale. Bonus points if they don't notice.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 1,128 feet (344 metres) tall and was designed by Bruce Graham and Fazlur Rahman Khan. When it topped out on 6 May 1968, it was the second-tallest building in the world. It holds offices, restaurants and about 700 homes, plus the 360 Chicago observation deck, with views over the city and up to four states.

card.hook: The Adler looks serious and formal, but put a whole lake and a row of skyscrapers behind it and it relaxes into a very good photo. Walk away from it a little and you'll see what we mean.

card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if you're close, because that sign is tall. Switch to 1x for a natural look, or 2x and up (depending on your phone) to pick out the lettering without stepping into traffic.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the marquee, then slide the brightness down a little so the lights keep their colour and the letters stay readable.
card.best_time: Go at night, when the marquee and vertical sign are lit up and stand out most. Give yourself a few minutes to try two or three framings, because the best crop depends on how many people are about.
card.selfie_here: Step into the pedestrian median in the middle of State Street (watch the traffic signals), flip to the front camera and use 0.5x so the CHICAGO sign sits over your shoulder. card.rules_and_safety: State Street is busy, so cross only at the proper crossings, wait for the signal and don't linger in the road. Only use the median if it's safe to do so.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical sign up with one of them so it stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.good_to_know: The Chicago Theatre opened in 1921 as the flagship of the Balaban and Katz cinema chain. Architects Rapp and Rapp gave it a Neo-Baroque French-revival style, and it's now the oldest surviving grand movie palace. It became a Chicago Landmark in 1983 and today is a performing arts venue with around 3,600 seats.

card.hook: Tribune Tower is so tall and so detailed that the pavement right under it is useless for photos, because it's too narrow to fit the whole thing in. Step back onto the bridge and it all falls into place.
card.stand_here: Stand at the midpoint of DuSable Bridge and face north. The tower rises ahead and slightly to your right, with its Gothic crown and buttresses against the sky.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full tower from the bridge. Then tap 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tight shot of the crown and buttresses. Save zoom 0.5x for when you're close to the base or down on the Riverwalk.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone upright and level so the tower's vertical lines stay straight, because tilting back makes it lean.
card.best_time: Midday to afternoon usually gives nice even light on the front when you face north. After dark, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked in and your phone still, so the lit-up buttresses come out sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the Chicago Riverwalk at the south end of DuSable Bridge, near the Wrigley Building, or the north end of the bridge where Michigan Avenue meets the bridge deck. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it) and tuck the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the plaza in front of the Wrigley Building, across North Michigan Avenue, while you pose with the full tower behind you (check the plaza when you get there, as the view from the sidewalk can be tight).
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to exterior shots, as the inside is generally not open for photography. The building is now residential, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.
card.challenge: Get the whole crown in the frame with a little sky above it and the tower's lines perfectly straight. Let the gridlines be your referee.
card.good_to_know: Tribune Tower is a neo-Gothic skyscraper at 435 North Michigan Avenue, 36 floors and about 141 metres (463 feet) tall. It was finished in 1925 after a famous 1922 design competition that drew more than 260 entries. The winning design by John Mead Howells and Raymond Hood took its crown from the 'butter tower' of Rouen Cathedral, and since 2018 the building has been converted into homes.

card.rules_and_safety: Drones are not allowed over Millennium Park or the pavilion. The pavilion and lawn can close during some scheduled concerts and events, so check the Millennium Park schedule on the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a shot where the criss-crossing steel lines above the lawn and the smooth curves of the shell both fit in one frame.
card.good_to_know: The pavilion opened on 16 July 2004 and holds up to 11,000 people. It's home to the Grant Park Music Festival, a free outdoor classical series. Frank Gehry designed the pavilion and the BP Bridge too, partly to shut out street noise from the pavilion.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on BP Bridge, on the east side of the pavilion, and face back west toward the stage, with the pavilion to the north-west of you. Photographers say it's less crowded than the straight-on view from the seating area.

card.hook: Most people walk into the Chicago Cultural Center for a quick look and end up staring at the ceiling for ten minutes. Fair enough: there are two stained-glass domes up there.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Chicago Cultural Center, where the phone icon on the map sits. Most of your photos happen in the entrance halls and rooms, or on the pavement outside.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the domes, the big marble halls and the staircases. Switch to 1x for the façade and tidy room views, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out mosaics and bronze details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on the glass of a dome, then slide the brightness down a touch so the colours stay rich and the glass doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when natural light comes through the stained glass. Earlier in the day is usually calmer indoors.
card.selfie_here: Head to Preston Bradley Hall on the third floor, on the south side near Washington Street, and stand with the Tiffany dome directly behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, so the dome fits over your shoulder. The Washington Street lobby staircase, with the marble and mosaics behind you, is a good second backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Michigan Avenue on the Millennium Park side and frame the full façade, while you pose on the pavement in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos for your own use don't need a permit. No photos in gallery spaces or where an event is on, no flash near the domes, and no drones. A wedding can close Preston Bradley Hall, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and find the most perfectly symmetrical shot you can of a dome or a marble staircase.
card.good_to_know: The building opened in 1897 as Chicago's main library and a Civil War memorial hall, and became an arts centre in 1978. The Tiffany dome in Preston Bradley Hall is about 12 metres across, and the Cultural Center calls it the largest Tiffany dome in the world. Outside, the west façade carries the 2017 mural "Rush More" by Kerry James Marshall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Chicago Cultural Center, where the phone icon on the map sits. Most of your photos happen in the entrance halls and rooms, or on the pavement outside.

card.hook: LaSalle Street is basically a long hallway, and at the end of it sits a tower wearing a copper pyramid hat with a giant grain goddess on top. Streets rarely set up a shot this neatly for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of LaSalle Street and Adams Street, about three blocks north of the building, and face south down LaSalle. The office towers on both sides will frame the Board of Trade at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full, even view down the street. If the tower looks a bit small, tap 2x or higher (depends on your phone), and save 0.5x for when you're much closer and want a dramatic look up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on the middle vertical line, then tap the tower and slide darker if the bright sky is washing out the pale stone.
card.best_time: Early on a weekend morning is best, with less traffic and fewer parked cars in your picture.
card.selfie_here: Head to the corner of LaSalle Street and Jackson Boulevard, where visitors already take their photos of the building. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the tower over your shoulder, and check on the spot which way puts it behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Adams Street corner facing south, then stand a few steps down the pavement with your back to the tower so it rises behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement or a median while you shoot. Traffic on LaSalle is a real hazard, and standing in the road isn't worth the picture.
card.challenge: Can you get both sides of the street perfectly balanced, with the tower dead centre and the tall edges dead straight?
card.good_to_know: The Chicago Board of Trade Building is a 44-storey Art Deco tower, about 184 m (604 ft) tall, opened in 1930 and designed by Holabird & Root. The statue on top is Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain, and she's three storeys tall. It was Chicago's tallest building until 1965, and it became a Chicago Landmark in 1977 and a National Historic Landmark in 1978.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of LaSalle Street and Adams Street, about three blocks north of the building, and face south down LaSalle. The office towers on both sides will frame the Board of Trade at the far end.

card.hook: Picture a giant face on a 50-foot glass tower, puckering up and spitting water at the kids in the pool below. Welcome to Crown Fountain, where the art splashes back.
card.stand_here: Go to the phone icon on the map, right at the edge of the black granite pool in Millennium Park. Face one of the two glass towers, with the spray and pool in front of you and the Chicago skyline behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get one tower with the pool and spray in front. Tap 0.5x to fit both towers and the pool in one shot, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with a single face.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright screen face, then drag the brighter/darker slider down a little so the glowing face doesn't blow out to white.
card.best_time: Come near the end of the day or after dark, when the faces show up best. Midday sun makes the screens hard to see. The water only runs from May to October, but the faces are on all year.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the shallow edge of the reflecting pool with one tower behind you, so the giant face is over your shoulder. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and take a smiley one first, then another when the face spits.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand on the east side of the pool, halfway between the two towers, so both screens and the Michigan Avenue buildings fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The area around the pool can get slippery, so watch your step. Keep an eye on children playing in the water, and keep your phone out of the spray. Check the official Millennium Park site for current closures or water-feature rules.
card.challenge: Get a selfie with a tower's face right behind you, and press the button just as it starts to spit.
card.good_to_know: Spanish artist Jaume Plensa designed Crown Fountain, and it opened in July 2004. Two glass brick towers, each 50 feet (15.2 m) tall, face each other across the pool. Their screens show video faces of Chicago residents, which is why some people call it the "Squirting Faces".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the phone icon on the map, right at the edge of the black granite pool in Millennium Park. Face one of the two glass towers, with the spray and pool in front of you and the Chicago skyline behind it.

card.hook: Picture a giant pink wedding cake at the end of a leafy avenue, with a tall jet of water on top instead of a bride and groom. This spot is the calm way to see it, away from the crowded basin edge.
card.stand_here: Stand on Columbus Drive, on the stretch between the Art Institute of Chicago and Buckingham Fountain, and stay on the pavement. Face east: the fountain is straight down the avenue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the avenue, the trees and the fountain all together. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the fountain and the buildings behind it closer together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on the centre line with a row of trees on each side, and hold your phone level so the buildings behind don't lean.
card.best_time: Go between roughly mid-April and mid-October, when the jets are running. The evening shows have coloured lights, so use night mode and keep your elbows tucked in. In winter the basin is empty, so expect a plainer picture, though it's sometimes decorated with festive lights.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the lakeside (east) edge of the fountain basin, turn your back on the fountain and use the front camera with the skyline ahead of you. Try 0.5x so the fountain fits over your shoulder, and check the position on the ground, since guides disagree on which side has the best skyline.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the western approach to the fountain, while you stand in front of the fountain about 10 feet back, so it fills the frame with the skyline or Lake Michigan behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed, but commercial photography or videography may need a permit. Take your photos from the pavement and keep well clear of the traffic. On windy days the mist can drift well beyond the basin, so keep your phone dry.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the fountain's central jet looks like it's growing straight out of the tree-lined avenue, then try a Live Photo to catch the water moving.
card.good_to_know: Buckingham Fountain was dedicated in 1927 and is one of the largest fountains in the world. Its rococo 'wedding cake' style was inspired by the Latona Fountain at Versailles. The design stands for Lake Michigan, with four pairs of sea horses for the four states that border it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Columbus Drive, on the stretch between the Art Institute of Chicago and Buckingham Fountain, and stay on the pavement. Face east: the fountain is straight down the avenue.

card.hook: Picture a tiny limestone castle stuck in the middle of the Magnificent Mile's glass and shopping bags. That's the Chicago Water Tower, and it looks wonderfully out of place.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jane M. Byrne Plaza, on the south side of the tower with the plaza in front of you. Face the tower and you'll see its full limestone height with the Michigan Avenue buildings around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole tower with the buildings around it. If you're close and the top gets cut off, drop to 0.5x and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Then try 2x or more (it depends on your phone) for the little turrets and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then drag the brightness down a little if the bright sky is washing out the top of the tower, and switch on the gridlines to keep the tower standing straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the area is quieter. One guide also likes the lit-up views in the evening and in winter, though it doesn't name a best spot for them.
card.selfie_here: Try the south edge of the plaza, in front of the tower, with the Wrigley Building and Tribune Tower visible down Michigan Avenue. For a flowery frame, stand in front of the tower with the beds along its base around you if the flowers are out. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the tower over your shoulder. Check the angle on the spot, since it depends on where you stand.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of Michigan Avenue with the tower in frame while you pose in front of the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: Michigan Avenue is busy, so wait for a gap in traffic if you cross. Photos of the outside are generally fine for personal use. If you go into the City Gallery, check the signs about cameras, and note that it's sometimes listed as closed.
card.challenge: Take a shot where the tower stands perfectly straight on the gridlines, then one where you're so close it looks like it's toppling. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The tower was designed in 1869 and is about 56 metres tall. It survived the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 while the buildings next to it burned. It's the second-oldest water tower in the United States, at 806 N Michigan Ave.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jane M. Byrne Plaza, on the south side of the tower with the plaza in front of you. Face the tower and you'll see its full limestone height with the Michigan Avenue buildings around it.
